key_findings.conditions: Patients with gastrointestinal tumors receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)
key_findings.finding: The gut microbiome plays a significant role in modulating the efficacy of ICIs. Interventions such as probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and dietary changes are discussed as methods to improve or maintain intestinal flora structure.

key_findings.conditions: Use of probiotic interventions in combination with ICIs
key_findings.finding: Probiotic interventions are highlighted for their potential contribution to improving the therapeutic effect of ICIs, which may lead to prolonged survival time and reduced severity of immune-related adverse effects (irAEs).

problem_or_question: The paper addresses why immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy only benefits approximately one-third of patients with gastrointestinal tumors and investigates how the gut microbiome influences this efficacy. It aims to summarize existing knowledge on using microbiome modulation (probiotics, FMT, diet) to enhance ICI outcomes.
research_scope: The review focuses on the interaction between the gut microbiome and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in the context of gastrointestinal tumors. It covers the current status of ICB therapy, the role of the microbiome, and various intervention strategies including probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and dietary interventions.
work_summary: This paper is a narrative review discussing the relationship between the intestinal microbiome and the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in patients with gastrointestinal tumors. Given that ICI therapy benefits only about one-third of patients, the authors explore how intestinal microbes influence treatment outcomes. The article specifically discusses four aspects: the microbiome, ICIs, combined treatments for gastrointestinal tumors, and the regulation of the gut microbiome. A particular emphasis is placed on how probiotic interventions can improve ICI therapeutic effects, prolong patient survival, and reduce the severity of immune-related adverse events (irAEs).
